chapters.name: Chapter 1: Understanding climate risk on your farm

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What climate-smart agriculture means
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the three aims of climate-smart agriculture and judge whether a practice is climate-smart.
This lesson builds toward: Given practices used on your farm or in your village, you will explain the three aims of climate-smart agriculture and judge whether each practice is climate-smart, naming which aim each practice helps.
Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) is a way of choosing farming practices with climate change in mind. FAO describes three aims: raise productivity and incomes in a sustainable way; help farms and families adapt and build resilience to climate shocks; and reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions where possible.
FAO stresses that a practice does not have to do all three. For most smallholders, food and income come first; lower emissions are a bonus. A practice is climate-smart if it fits your farm and makes it more productive and more resilient.
Examples farmers in Africa already use: mulching and minimum tillage to keep soil moist, planting pits and water pans, drought-tolerant and early-maturing varieties, intercropping maize with beans or cowpea, push-pull for stemborers and fall armyworm, trees on farm, improved fodder, and crop or livestock insurance.
Words to know:
- Climate-smart agriculture (CSA): farming that raises productivity, helps farms adapt to climate change, and cuts emissions where possible.
- Resilience: the ability of a farm and family to cope with a shock, such as drought, and recover quickly.
- Adaptation: changing how you farm to cope with a changing climate.
Official sources:
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
Try it now: List three practices already used on your farm or in your village. For each, write which of the three CSA aims it helps (productivity, resilience, emissions).
You can now explain the three aims of climate-smart agriculture and judge whether a practice is climate-smart.

check.q: Which is a climate-smart practice farmers in Africa already use?
options: Planting only one crop every year
check.why: Mulching keeps soil moist and covered, helping productivity and resilience.

check.q: A practice raises your yields and helps you survive dry spells but does not cut emissions. Is it climate-smart?
options: No; it must do all three
Yes, if it fits your farm and improves productivity and resilience
Only if a government approves it
check.why: FAO says a practice does not have to meet all three aims; for smallholders, food and income come first.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading the official seasonal forecast
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find and use your national weather service's seasonal forecast to plan the season.
This lesson builds toward: Before a rainy season, you will find your national weather service's seasonal forecast and write two changes it means for your plan, noting what it says, the date you read it, and that it gives chances, not promises.
Before each rainy season, national weather services publish a seasonal forecast: whether rains are expected to be above, near or below normal, and when they may start and end. In Kenya, the Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) publishes seasonal forecasts and agrometeorological bulletins. In Nigeria, the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) publishes seasonal climate predictions. Other countries have their own services; many forecasts are also shared on radio and by extension officers.
A seasonal forecast gives chances, not promises. "Below normal" means a higher chance of less rain than usual in your area, not that it will certainly be dry. Use it to adjust, not to bet everything: for example choose a shorter-maturing variety, plant on the right date, plan water harvesting, or reduce area of a thirsty crop.
Use short-range forecasts (the next few days) for daily decisions such as when to plant after the rains start, when to spray or topdress, and when to harvest and dry.
Step by step:
- Find your national weather service's website, radio slot or extension bulletin.
- Read the seasonal forecast for your county or state.
- Note: above, near or below normal; expected start and end of rains.
- Write two changes you will make because of it.
- Check short-range forecasts for planting, topdressing and harvest days.
Words to know:
- Seasonal forecast: an outlook of rainfall and temperature for the coming season, given as chances.
- Onset: the start of the rainy season.
- Agrometeorological bulletin: a weather report written for farmers, linking weather to crops.
Official sources:
- Kenya Meteorological Department (seasonal forecasts, agrometeorological bulletins)
- Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet)
Try it now: Find the latest seasonal forecast for your area from KMD, NiMet or your country's weather service. Write what it says, the date you read it, and two changes you will make to your plan.
You can now find the official seasonal forecast and use it to adjust your season plan.

check.q: What does a seasonal forecast tell you?
options: The exact rain on each day
Whether rains are likely above, near or below normal
check.why: A seasonal forecast gives the chances of above, near or below normal rain and when rains may start and end.

check.q: The forecast says rains may end early. What is a sensible change?
check.why: A shorter-maturing variety can finish before the rains end.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Drawing your farm's climate-risk calendar
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw a month-by-month calendar of the climate risks your farm faces.
This lesson builds toward: For your own farm or an example farm, you will draw a month-by-month climate-risk calendar and circle the danger points, with seasons, farm jobs, risks and at least two danger points marked.
A climate-risk calendar puts your crops and animals next to the risks of each month. Draw 12 columns for the months. In the first row, write your seasons (long rains, short rains, dry season, or wet and dry season in much of Nigeria). Below, write what you do each month: land preparation, planting, weeding, topdressing, harvest, drying, selling, and when animals need most feed and water.
Then mark the risks: late onset or early end of rains, dry spells in the middle of the season, heavy storms and floods, heat at flowering, pests and diseases that follow weather (fall armyworm, aphids, fungal diseases in wet spells), and post-harvest losses when grain is stored damp.
Look for the danger points: the months when an important job meets a big risk, such as maize flowering in a month that often has a dry spell. Those are where climate-smart practices help most. Ask older farmers how the pattern has changed over the years.
Step by step:
- Draw 12 month columns; write your seasons.
- Write your farm jobs and animal needs by month.
- Mark the climate risks and weather-linked pests.
- Circle the danger points where a key job meets a big risk.
- Ask older farmers what has changed.
Words to know:
- Dry spell: a period of days or weeks without useful rain during the rainy season.
- Danger point: a time when an important farm job meets a high climate risk.
Official sources:
- FAO GIEWS Earth Observation (drought and vegetation indicators)
Try it now: Draw the climate-risk calendar for your farm on paper or in a phone spreadsheet. Circle at least two danger points.
You can now draw a climate-risk calendar for your farm and find its danger points.

check.q: What goes in the rows below the months on a climate-risk calendar?
options: Your farm jobs, animal needs and the risks
check.why: The calendar puts farm jobs and animal needs next to each month's risks.

check.q: You store maize in a month that is often wet. What do you mark?
options: A post-harvest loss risk from damp grain
check.why: Grain stored damp in wet months is a post-harvest loss risk.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Keeping soil and water on the farm
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose soil and water practices that fit your farm and slope.
This lesson builds toward: Given the slope and water flow on your farm, you will choose soil and water practices that fit and plan a small test, comparing the tested area with your usual way.
Healthy soil holds more water and feeds crops through dry spells. Three conservation agriculture principles help: disturb the soil as little as possible (minimum tillage), keep it covered (crop residue or mulch instead of burning), and rotate or intercrop (for example maize with beans, cowpea or pigeon pea). Add manure or compost to build organic matter.
Catch rain where it falls. Planting pits or basins (called zai in the Sahel) collect water and manure around each plant. Tied ridges and contour bunds stop water running off. On slopes, terraces such as fanya juu in Kenya, grass strips and trees along contours stop erosion. Water pans and roof catchment store water for animals, nurseries and kitchen gardens.
Start small: try a practice on one part of the field, compare it with your usual way, and keep what works. Ask your extension officer for local designs and labour needs.
Step by step:
- Stop burning residue; leave it as mulch.
- Reduce ploughing where weeds can be managed.
- Rotate or intercrop with a legume.
- Catch rain: planting pits, tied ridges, contour bunds.
- On slopes: terraces, grass strips, trees on contours.
- Try on a small area first and compare.
Words to know:
- Conservation agriculture: farming with minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and crop rotation.
- Mulch: a layer of crop residue, grass or leaves on the soil to keep it moist and cool.
- Zai pits / planting basins: small pits that collect rainwater and manure around plants.
- Fanya juu: a Kenyan terrace made by throwing soil uphill from a ditch to form a bank.
Official sources:
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
Try it now: Walk your farm after rain or look at it now. Mark where water runs off, where soil is washing away, and where water stands. Choose one soil or water practice for one spot and write how you will test it.
You can now choose and test soil and water practices that keep moisture and soil on your farm.

check.q: What are tied ridges and contour bunds for?
options: Stopping water running off the field
check.why: They hold rain on the field so it soaks in instead of running off.

check.q: Water rushes down your sloping field after rain and carries soil. What do you choose?
options: Plough up and down the slope
Grass strips or terraces along the contours
check.why: Terraces and grass strips on contours stop erosion on slopes.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Choosing crops and varieties that cope
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick crops, varieties and planting strategies that reduce climate risk.
This lesson builds toward: Given your main crop and local risks, you will choose certified drought-tolerant or early varieties, a drought-hardy crop and a planting strategy that reduce risk, buying seed only from registered dealers.
Varieties matter. CGIAR's maize research center CIMMYT and partners have bred drought-tolerant maize varieties released across many countries in sub-Saharan Africa; CGIAR reports they can yield clearly more than conventional varieties under drought. Early-maturing beans and maize escape late-season drought. Ask your agrovet or extension officer which certified varieties suit your area, and buy certified seed from registered dealers.
Crops matter too. Sorghum, millet, cassava, cowpea and pigeon pea cope with dry conditions better than maize in many areas. Growing more than one crop, and intercropping, spreads risk: if one fails, another may succeed.
Pests change with the climate. Push-pull, developed by icipe with partners, intercrops maize or sorghum with desmodium and borders it with Napier or Brachiaria grass; icipe reports it sharply reduces stemborer, striga and fall armyworm damage. Stagger planting dates in small blocks, and plant promptly at the true onset of rains.
Step by step:
- Ask extension or an agrovet for certified drought-tolerant or early varieties for your area.
- Buy certified seed from a registered dealer.
- Add a drought-hardy crop (sorghum, cassava, cowpea, pigeon pea).
- Intercrop to spread risk; consider push-pull for maize or sorghum.
- Plant promptly at true onset; stagger small blocks.
Words to know:
- Drought-tolerant variety: a crop variety bred to yield better than others when water is short.
- Early-maturing: ready to harvest sooner, so it can escape late-season drought.
- Certified seed: seed checked by the official seed authority for purity and quality.
- Push-pull: a system where desmodium repels pests from maize or sorghum and border grass attracts them away.
Official sources:
- CGIAR: Climate-smart (drought-tolerant) maize
- icipe: Push-pull technology halts fall armyworm
Try it now: For your main crop, find one drought-tolerant or early-maturing certified variety sold near you (ask an agrovet or extension officer), and choose one drought-hardy crop to add. Write where you will plant each.
You can now choose crops, varieties and planting strategies that lower your farm's climate risk.

check.q: Why do early-maturing varieties help in dry areas?
check.why: Early-maturing crops finish before late-season drought hits.

check.q: Your maize often fails in dry years. What adds a safety net?
options: Add a drought-hardy crop like sorghum or cowpea
Buy uncertified seed in the market
check.why: Growing more than one crop, including a drought-hardy one, spreads risk.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Trees, livestock and insurance: spreading the risk
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Add at least one way to spread risk beyond your main crop, then write your plan.
This lesson builds toward: Beyond your main crop, you will plan at least one way to spread risk with trees, livestock feed and water, or insurance, checking any insurance trigger and that the insurer is licensed.
Trees on farms (agroforestry) give shade, windbreaks, fodder, fruit, fuel and timber, protect soil, and store carbon. Fruit trees such as mango and avocado, nitrogen-fixing trees, and boundary trees can all add income that does not depend on one season's rains.
Livestock can be a buffer, but also suffer in drought. Plant and store fodder (Napier, Brachiaria, crop residues, hay), protect water sources, choose hardy breeds, and keep animal numbers in line with the feed you can grow or buy. Small stock such as goats and poultry can be easier to keep through dry years.
Insurance moves part of the risk to an insurer. Weather-index and area-yield insurance pay out when rainfall or area yields fall below a set level, and are sold in some areas through cooperatives, input dealers or mobile money. Ask your cooperative or extension officer, read what triggers a payout, and check the insurer is licensed by your insurance regulator (in Kenya the Insurance Regulatory Authority, in Nigeria NAICOM). Savings groups and diversified income also spread risk.
Step by step:
- Choose trees that fit your farm: fruit, fodder, boundary or nitrogen-fixing.
- Plan fodder and water for animals through the dry season.
- Match animal numbers to the feed you can grow or buy.
- Ask about weather-index or area-yield insurance; read the payout trigger; check the insurer is licensed.
- Write your climate-smart plan.
Words to know:
- Agroforestry: growing trees together with crops or livestock on the same land.
- Fodder: plants grown or kept to feed animals.
- Weather-index insurance: insurance that pays when a weather measure, such as rainfall, falls below a set level.
- Payout trigger: the condition that makes the insurer pay.
Official sources:
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page climate-smart plan: risk calendar, this season's forecast and the date you read it, and at least five practices (soil and water, crops and varieties, spreading risk), with start dates and how you will judge success.
You can now use trees, livestock, insurance and savings to spread climate risk, and write a complete climate-smart plan for your farm.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Climate-risk calendar Months, jobs or risks missing, or no danger points. Twelve months with seasons, farm jobs, risks and at least two danger points circled. Includes what older farmers say has changed. Seasonal forecast No forecast, or no date or source. What this season's official forecast says, its source and the date it was read. Shows two plan changes made because of the forecast. Soil and water practice No soil or water practice. At least one soil or water practice that fits the farm, with a start date. Planned as a small test compared with the usual way. Crops and varieties No crop or variety practice. At least one variety or crop practice that reduces risk, with certified seed from a registered dealer. Also includes intercropping or push-pull where it fits. Spreading risk No way to spread risk beyond the main crop. At least one tree, livestock or insurance practice, with a start date. For insurance, names the payout trigger and checks the insurer is licensed. Five practices and success measures Fewer than five practices, or no way to judge success. At least five practices, each with when to start and how you will know if it worked. Notes which climate-smart aim each practice helps. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Growing trees together with crops or livestock
check.why: Agroforestry means trees on farms with crops or animals.

check.q: A dry season is coming and you keep goats and cows. What do you plan?
options: Fodder and water, with animal numbers matched to feed
check.why: Planning fodder and water and matching numbers to feed protects animals in drought.
